extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, disciplinary counsel, and USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline participants
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state bar's disciplinary adjudication (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)), including the Selling v. Radford factors and related professional-responsibility rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline standard (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[T]he USPTO Director shall consider any timely filed response and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i)-(iv)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation codifies the Selling presumption: a state's disciplinary adjudication creates a presumption that identical federal discipline is proper unless one of the enumerated defenses is shown. The respondent bears the burden to produce clear and convincing evidence of a genuine issue of material fact on one of the listed grounds. The USPTO is not sitting as a court of review to relitigate state factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: (i) Due process deprivation (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: "The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires meaningful notice of charges and a meaningful opportunity to be heard (e.g., to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, have counsel, and subpoena witnesses). Mere dissatisfaction with outcomes, routine discovery or evidentiary rulings, or the use of videographed depositions (where permitted) does not itself establish deprivation. Failure to raise or pursue appellate remedies may undermine a due-process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: (ii) Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: "There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a demanding standard — more than disputing the factfinder's weighing or credibility determinations. The respondent must show substantial flaws in the proof such that acceptance of the state finding would be untenable. Credibility findings and factual inferences of the state tribunal receive deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: (iii) Grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: "The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of grave injustice can include arguments that the state proceeding was outside its authority (e.g., exclusive federal jurisdiction). Such jurisdictional preemption is narrowly construed: state disciplinary proceedings concerning ethical obligations typically are not preempted by federal patent law (see Christianson, Sperry, Kroll). To succeed requires a clear and convincing showing of a substantial, outcome-determinative injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: (iv) No public sanction was imposed by the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state did not in fact impose a public sanction of the listed types, that can defeat imposition of identical federal discipline. The USPTO will check the nature of the state sanction before imposing reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner must "clearly and convincingly" demonstrate that one of the Selling/§11.24 defenses applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal cases interpret this burden narrowly; courts and the USPTO expect clear and convincing evidence, and the respondent bears this burden. Citations include Selling v. Radford, In re Kramer, and In re Friedman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] practitioner shall not ... [e]ngage in any conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulation provides a ground for Office discipline where a state disciplinary finding shows conduct that reflects adversely on an attorney's fitness to practice before the USPTO. A state censure predicated on such misconduct can support a USPTO censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to former clients (Rule 1.9(c)(1) of state RPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] lawyer who has formerly represented a client in a matter ... shall not thereafter: (1) use information relating to the representation to the disadvantage of the former client except as these Rules would permit ... or (2) reveal information relating to the representation except as these Rules would permit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State professional-conduct rules forbid using or revealing confidential information obtained while representing a former client to that client's disadvantage. Comment 8 clarifies that whether information is "generally known" depends on how it was acquired; public availability does not automatically negate confidentiality. Violations can lead to state discipline that supports reciprocal USPTO discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due-process factual particulars accepted as satisfying (guidance from cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific elements constituting meaningful opportunity to be heard: notice of charges, participation in discovery, right to testify, present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, make objections, and present appellate challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., In re Squire, Mathews v. Eldridge, In re Zdravkovich) holds that attendance and active participation in hearings, ability to call/cross-examine witnesses, and the availability of counsel and appeal procedures satisfy due process. Tactical choices (e.g., not subpoenaing witnesses) preclude later claims of prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state factfinding; limited federal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal/USPTO review is limited; the agency (like federal courts) does not relitigate credibility or reweigh evidence and should defer to state tribunals unless one of the narrow Selling exceptions is met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent (In re Zdravkovich, In re Sibley, In re Kramer) emphasizes narrow review. A disagreement over credibility or evidentiary weight is insufficient to overturn a state disciplinary finding under § 11.24(d)(1)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: State vs. federal jurisdiction preemption standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An action 'arises under' patent law when federal patent law creates the cause of action or the plaintiff's right to relief necessarily depends on resolution of a substantial question of federal patent law (Christianson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State disciplinary actions based on breaches of state-imposed ethical duties generally do not present exclusive federal jurisdiction even if related to patent matters (Sperry; Kroll). The USPTO's ethics regulations explicitly do not preempt state authority to regulate the practice of law except to the extent necessary for the Office to accomplish federal objectives (37 C.F.R. § 10.1).
